{{Short description|Austrian philosopher and psychologist}}
[[File:Hoefler.jpg|thumb|Alois Höfler]]

'''Alois Höfler''' ({{IPA|de|ˈhøːflɐ|lang}}; April 6, 1853 – February 26, 1922) was an Austrian [[philosopher]] and university professor of education. He was seen by the logical positivist [[Otto Neurath]] as an important link between [[Bernard Bolzano]]'s work and the [[Vienna Circle]].

== Biography ==
Alois Höfler was born in [[Kirchdorf an der Krems|Kirchdorf]] in Upper Austria. His father and mother died while he was in his early and middle teens. He and his two younger sisters were then raised by a second mother, Amalie Boheim.{{sfn|Blackmore|Itagaki|Tanaka|2001|p=237}} He had four sons with his wife Auguste Dornhöffer,{{sfn|Blackmore|Itagaki|Tanaka|2001|p=239}} including [[Otto Höfler]].{{sfn|Heinrich|2010}}

In the fall of 1871, Höfler entered the [[University of Vienna]] where he studied mathematics and physics with [[Ludwig Boltzmann]] and [[Josef Stefan]].{{sfn|Blackmore|Itagaki|Tanaka|2001|p=236}} After his teaching examination in 1876 at the age of 23, he taught in the Josefstädter-[[Gymnasium (school)|gymnasium]] and other gymnasiums (advanced secondary schools) in [[Vienna]].{{sfn|Blackmore|Itagaki|Tanaka|2001|p=237}}{{sfn|Höfer|1994}} He received his doctoral degree at Vienna in 1885,{{sfn|Blackmore|Itagaki|Tanaka|2001|p=239}}{{sfn|Reichert|1972}} under [[Alexius Meinong]]'s remote supervision,{{sfn|Dewalque|2017}}{{sfn|Blackmore|Itagaki|Tanaka|2001|pp=240}} with a thesis titled ''Some Laws of Incompatibility between Judgments'' (''Einige Gesetze der Unverträglichkeiten zwischen Urteilen'').{{sfn|Blackmore|Itagaki|Tanaka|2001|p=239}}{{sfn|Reichert|1972}} He received his [[habilitation]] at Vienna in 1894{{sfn|Dewalque|2017}} with a thesis titled ''Psychic Work'' (''Psychische Arbeit'').{{sfn|Rollinger|1999}}{{sfn|Reichert|1972}}

During the 1870s and 1880s Höfler also attended evening classes taught by [[Franz Brentano]] and Meinong. His philosophical view was strongly influenced by Meinong. From 1881 to 1903 he taught mathematics, physics and philosophical propaedeutics at the grammar school of the [[Theresian Academy]] in Vienna.{{sfn|Reichert|1972}} He became professor of philosophy and pedagogy at the [[German University of Prague]] in 1903 (as successor to [[Otto Willmann]]) and at the University of Vienna in 1907 (as successor to Theodor Vogt).{{sfn|Blackmore|Itagaki|Tanaka|2001|p=264}}{{sfn|Fisette|2021}}

His increasing interest in philosophy and in making it more scientific led him to study and write increasingly on logic and psychology as well.  In the opinion of the ardent [[logical positivism|logical positivist]] [[Otto Neurath]],  through his involvement in the [[School of Brentano]], Höfler was an important connection  between the work on logic of [[Bernard Bolzano]] and the [[Vienna Circle]].{{sfn|Fisette|2014}}{{sfn|Miskiewicz|2005}} In 1914, he reprinted the 77 years old Bolzano's ''Theory of Science'', which was said to be almost impossible to find at the time.{{sfn|Anonymous|1914}} He also loved music, poetry, and the arts. He strongly opposed attempting to reduce their role in schools.{{sfn|Blackmore|Itagaki|Tanaka|2001|p=239}}

Höfler died in Vienna.
